structure.title: Books 1–4 · The family takes a dispute to the monastery
structure.text: A family dispute about money brings a father and his sons to the monastery for a meeting with an elder. The visit gives Fyodor Pavlovich a fresh audience for his buffoonery. The people who came to make peace start having to decide whose humiliation they are prepared to watch.

structure.title: Books 5–7 · Ivan and Alyosha at table
structure.text: Over a meal Ivan offers his brother a case against accepting a world bought at the price of children's suffering. His story of the Grand Inquisitor puts Christ back on earth among men who have built their authority in his name. Alyosha must answer someone he loves.

structure.title: Books 8–9 · A desperate search for money
structure.text: As Dmitri rushes from one possible rescuer to another, promises, threats and sums of money begin to leave a trail of witnesses. What each witness actually saw will matter considerably more than anybody supposes in the heat of the evening.

structure.title: Book 10 – epilogue · A case in court and a circle of schoolboys
structure.text: Lawyers give the town two remarkably persuasive histories of the same family. Beside the public proceedings runs Alyosha's quieter involvement with a group of boys. They too know what it means to join a crowd against one person.

people.name: Dmitri
people.text: He wants to account for money he owes and to believe he is an honourable man. The very people from whom he seeks proof of his honour have heard him boast, threaten and contradict himself.

people.name: Ivan and Alyosha
people.role: Brothers who take each other seriously
people.text: Ivan trusts his refusal to excuse cruelty. Alyosha has learned from the elder Zosima to begin with the person within reach. Neither can dismiss the other as stupid or indifferent. Their affection makes their disagreements difficult to escape.

people.name: Smerdyakov
people.text: He hears the family's arguments from a position the brothers scarcely consider. An idea that sounds brilliantly hypothetical at dinner can suggest possibilities of action to the man expected to serve the meal.

context.title: What a starets does
context.text: People come to Zosima for guidance in grief, domestic trouble and questions of conscience. His authority depends on their willingness to disclose what is shameful. Fyodor Pavlovich recognises the occasion as an opportunity to perform shame in front of spectators.

context.title: Ivan’s entrance ticket
context.text: Ivan asks his brother to imagine being offered a final harmony that would reconcile all the world’s suffering. His refusal turns on the price paid by children who could never consent. It matters that he offers this thought to Alyosha, whose answer cannot be separated from how he treats children he actually knows.

passages.quote: I hasten to give back my entrance ticket

notice.text: Compare confessing an impulse with admitting an act.
notice.why: A brother may take responsibility for a wish or a suggestion another person acted on. Such confessions have enormous moral weight and can be quite misleading when treated as answers to a policeman's question.

notice.text: Follow the listeners out of the room.
notice.why: An idea voiced by Ivan changes as it travels into another person's account of what he authorised. Dostoevsky allows overhearers the power to do something with an argument its author would never have chosen.

opening: The Karamazov brothers have a father who treats humiliation as entertainment and gives them ample reason to hate him. One brother is consumed by jealousy, another cannot accept a world that permits children to suffer, and the youngest is trying to live by love. Money and desire bring their arguments dangerously close to action. Dostoevsky lets the dispute over God take place among people who must still face one another at breakfast, owe debts, make accusations, and wonder what they secretly wished would happen.
